newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EMU seen prompting target zones for G3 currencies.
newsitem.headline: EMU seen prompting target zones for G3 currencies.

text.p: Target zones for the world's major currencies may be the best way of managing the new monetary order that emerges with a single European currency, Belgian Finance Minister Philippe Maystadt said on Thursday.
Such a revamped currency regime would also include an important role for the International Monetary Fund (IMF) in promoting stability between the euro, the dollar and the yen.

"There will be a case for monitoring the movements of exchange rates among the reserve currencies of the system...in order to detect marked misalignments," Maystadt said in a speech to London's Royal Institute for International Affairs, a copy of which was made available in Brussels.
Closer cooperation in detecting currency "misalignments" could be aided by the IMF in collaboration with countries joining economic and monetary union (EMU), the United States and Japan.

"It would be suitable for the IMF to review, regularly together with the authorities of those countries, exchange rate developments and, if necessary, to convince the countries concerned to take measures to resolve misalignments developing among the three currencies," he added.
Although Maystadt did not see a return to fixed-rate monetary order, management of the three major reserve currencies, perhaps in the form of target zones, might be desirable
"Till now, it has not been possible to find the degree of consensus necessary to renew thinking on a reform of the present system of generalised floating," Maystadt said.

"This is not to say that the world should return to a fixed rate system. I am however convinced that it might become useful, at some time, to declare what could be considered as 'target zone' or, in more cautious terms, 'plausibility zones'."

Although the introduction of the euro would eventually rival the dollar on global markets, the Belgian minister, who is also Chairman of the IMF's interim committee, did not see this happening quickly.
The dollar's widespread use in world trade and the time it would take to develop a deep and liquid financial market in the euro should allow the U.S. currency to retain a pre-eminent role.
But as a warning to U.S. officials about being complacent about the international effects of EMU, Maystadt said greater attention would be needed as the euro grows in importance.

"I would like to say that the United States will be obliged to take dollar fluctuations more seriously following the creation of the euro, because, as time goes by, the euro, backed by the world's largest single economy, will become a credible substitute for the dollar," Maystadt said.
